Issue 1: Rapid Decline in Children As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the Shinooka area has fallen to less than half compared to 20 years ago. Meanwhile, the population aged 65 and over has increased approximately 2.5 times. Issue 2: Aging Facilities Shinooka Elementary School was built in 1958 (over 60 years ago), and Shinooka Junior High School was built in 1965 (about 60 years ago). Other schools are similarly aging. Issue 3: Shift to Single-Class Grades If current trends continue, by 2033, all elementary schools and Shinooka Junior High School in the Shinooka area are projected to have only one class per grade. Based on official city documents, a parent survey (July 2025, 471 respondents), and discussions at the "Think About Schools" meetings, here are the main expected benefits of the school reorganization. Class Reshuffles Become Possible With one class per grade, students spend all 6 years of elementary school and 3 years of junior high with the same classmates. After reorganization, schools will be large enough to reshuffle classes every year, preventing relationships from becoming rigid. 66.4% of parents cited fixed social dynamics as a current concern. Exposure to Diverse Peers & Perspectives Daily interaction with more classmates creates an environment where children naturally encounter diverse ways of thinking and values. In the parent survey, 52.2% hoped for opportunities to develop independence and teamwork in a group, while 48.6% wanted an environment with more friends. Richer Extracurricular Activities More students means more clubs, committees, and activities to choose from. This was the #1 expectation (55.2%) among parents in the survey — the top benefit cited for reorganization. Nine Years of Connected Learning (Grades 1–9) The four reorganized schools will operate as "Shinooka Gakuen" with a unified 9-year curriculum. Stronger elementary–junior high coordination is expected to ease the "middle school transition gap." 46.1% of parents expect improved academic and life guidance through this coordination. Stronger Teaching Staff Small schools struggle to maintain a well-balanced mix of experienced and specialist teachers. Larger schools enable better staffing, allowing diverse teaching expertise to be fully utilized. Updated School Facilities Shinooka Elementary School was built in 1958 — now 67 years old; Shinooka Junior High in 1965. Reorganization allows the city to carry out planned replacements and provide students with safe, modern learning environments. 📊 Parent Survey (July 2025, 471 responses) — Top expectations for reorganization: 🥇 Wider range of clubs & extracurricular activities 55.2% 🥈 Opportunities to develop independence & teamwork 52.2% 🥉 An environment with more friends 48.6% 📄 Source: Komaki City School Reorganization Official Page
Learning and Support after the Reorganization

A summary of what the city has said in its published material about teaching after the reorganization, classes and teachers, support during the transition, and health and safety. All of it is rewritten by this site from the city's material. The core of teaching: “learning together” The city has long practiced “learning together” — lessons in which children listen to each other and deepen their learning by accepting each other's ideas. In the city's view this works best with groups large enough to meet a range of ways of thinking and values. At the same time, the city accepts that small schools have the advantage of keeping every child in view. School size and class size The city's optimal size is 12–24 classes per school for both elementary and junior high (2–4 classes per grade in elementary, 4–8 in junior high). The city added to the plan that optimal size means the number of classes, not the number of children per class, and that it has no intention of rejecting small classes. The maximum class size is 35 for every elementary grade and the first year of junior high, and 40 for the second and third years; Aichi Prefecture plans to lower the second and third years to 35 in stages from FY2026. The national government also changed the law in 2026, setting the junior high standard at 35 (phased in until FY2027). The city told the city council that a class size of about 21–25 children, large enough to allow classes to be reshuffled, needs to be secured. Teachers The city says that staff numbers will rise as pupil numbers rise with the reorganization, and that it is working with the prefecture so that staff can be placed as planned for FY2027. Staff numbers at public elementary and junior high schools are calculated from the number of classes under national law (the Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers). Support during the transition So that the change does not weigh on children, exchanges between schools are under way before the reorganization (in elementary schools, hands-on arts and culture lessons and an exchange in Tokadai Central Park; in junior high, joint satoyama conservation and arts appreciation by Shinooka and Hikarigaoka Junior High). The city also states that it will publicize and strengthen counseling by each school's counselors and school counselors, pass on information and support methods for children who need support, and maintain special-needs classes and resource-room instruction. The city also told the city council that it is considering opening a comprehensive education support center for children not attending school, with closed school buildings as one candidate site (not yet decided). Where the new schools' content is decided Since July 2025 a preparatory research committee has been discussing the new schools' curriculum, educational goals, school song, emblem, clubs and more. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 4). Health and safety As a heatstroke measure, the city says it is installing bottle-refill water dispensers in every elementary and junior high school for use from summer 2026 (same, No. 5). By law, elementary and junior high schools have a school nurse-teacher (the health-room teacher) (School Education Act). The gyms and grounds of closing schools are expected to remain in use as evacuation shelters and sites from FY2027 onward. 🔎 This site's own review and proposals on how academic ability, personal strengths, subject-by-subject abilities, health and more could change with the reorganization are on the Review & ideas page (not the city's view).

Outlook after Phase 1: If student numbers continue to decline after Phase 1 (FY2027), further consolidation into 1 elementary and 1 junior high school may be considered, along with the introduction of integrated elementary-junior high education. The decision on Phase 2 will be made based on the situation following Phase 1. What the city says about integrated elementary–junior high education: As advantages, the city lists systematic learning across nine years, easing the stumble on entering junior high, and continuing support suited to each child; as drawbacks, the loss of the break between elementary and junior high, fewer chances for older elementary pupils to develop leadership and independence, and a possible increase in teachers' paperwork. It says it will start with elementary–junior high cooperation and consider a move to integrated education while listening carefully to schools and parents.

School Buildings The buildings of closed schools are generally planned to be demolished. Gymnasium & School Grounds Gymnasiums and school grounds are generally planned to be kept. They are expected to be used for local sports and community activities. They will be maintained from FY2027 onward and are expected to remain designated as evacuation shelters and sites.

Plain-language notes on the words that keep coming up in this plan. Switching to the kids view makes the sentences simpler but leaves these words in place, so look them up here. School reorganization Combining schools that have grown small as the number of children falls. In the Shinooka district, five elementary schools are to become two and three junior high schools are to become two in FY2027. Appropriate school size The size a school ought to be. The national standard is 2–3 classes per year group (12–18 in total) for both elementary and junior high. It is about the number of classes, not the number of children in one class. Komaki City takes 12–24 classes per school as its optimal size. Integrated elementary–junior high education Elementary and junior high schools planning their nine years together as one continuous education. It does not necessarily mean one shared building. Compulsory education school A single school combining elementary and junior high. It runs from year 1 to year 9 and has one principal. School district Which school a child attends based on where they live. It is decided by address. Public comment A process where the city shows a draft plan first and collects opinions from residents. The opinions and the city’s replies are published. The Shinooka plan drew 142 comments from 55 people. Community council A body of local residents set up for each elementary school district. It discusses and runs things for the area, such as festivals and disaster preparedness. Moving club activities to the community Handing club activities, long supervised by teachers, over to community clubs and organizations. The national government says this starts in FY2026. “Meeting to think about our schools” A forum the city set up to discuss the reorganization with local residents. Five sessions were held in the Shinooka district in FY2025.

Besides Shinooka, school reorganization is also being discussed in other districts of Komaki and in neighboring Kasugai City. These are separate from the Shinooka plan; here we list only published facts. As of November 2026 ■ Other districts of Komaki Kitazato district (two elementary schools, one junior high) The city’s “New School-Building Promotion Plan” named it, together with Shinooka and Habashita (巾下), as a district where reorganization talks should start right away. “Kitazato District School Meetings” were held in July and October 2026. The direction (draft) the city presented is to merge the three schools into one and build a new school, premised on combined elementary–junior high education, on the grounds of Kitazato Elementary and Kitazato Junior High. The city says there is no need to reorganize in a hurry using the existing buildings, as in Shinooka, but because every building is aging, rebuilding and reorganization will be discussed together. Its schedule: a survey of pupils and parents and a third meeting during FY2026, and by March 2027 the selection of a firm to draw up the basic concept and plan for the new buildings. Questions in the city council are on the Council Deliberations page. Habashita (巾下) district (two elementary schools, one junior high) The promotion plan expects that by FY2033 Mitsubuchi (三ツ渕) Elementary will have one class in every grade and Komaki-Nishi Junior High two, and names the district, together with Shinooka and Kitazato, as one where reorganization talks should start right away. Muranaka (村中) and Mitsubuchi Elementary buildings are over 60 years old. Komaki, Komaki-Minami and Ajioka districts The promotion plan expects these districts to have many children, with every school meeting the city’s appropriate size until FY2033. However, Iwasaki Junior High in Ajioka is expected to fall below it in FY2038. Even in districts that keep all their schools, school zones may be revised along with a neighboring district’s reorganization. 🔄 The city’s school-reorganization pages for districts other than Shinooka (meetings and the like) are checked automatically every day and listed newest first (titles machine-translated). ■ Neighboring Kasugai City In February 2025 Kasugai City compiled its “Basic Approach to the Appropriate Size of Elementary and Junior High Schools” and made the Sakashita junior high school district and the four junior high school districts of the Kozoji New Town area its first priority. It considers at least two classes per grade necessary at both levels. Sakashita junior high school district (three elementary schools, one junior high) A basic policy toward merging was adopted in June 2026: the three elementary schools will become one, and Sakashita Junior High will not merge with other junior highs. At a September meeting the city presented its view: build a combined elementary–junior high school, with both on one site, on the Sakashita Junior High grounds (also acquiring the adjacent land), aiming to open in FY2033 or FY2034. A panel of parents, local representatives and school staff continues to discuss the details. Kozoji New Town area (Fujiyamadai, Iwanaridai, Takamoridai and Ishiodai junior high school districts) Public comments were invited on the interim draft of the basic policy toward merging, and 23 people sent 44 comments (results published in October 2026). The draft splits the area into two — “Fujiyamadai–Iwanaridai” and “Takamoridai–Ishiodai” — and will consider in each how many schools to merge and in what combination. Four junior highs and nine elementary schools are covered. Panels will be set up for each area to discuss, including whether merging is needed at all, and a plan will be drawn up if schools are merged. 🔄 Kasugai City’s pages are checked automatically every day; the five most recently updated are listed (titles as on Kasugai’s pages, machine-translated outside Japanese). Review: what the plan does not say

Part 1 Examining the plan itself Key points 🔎1–5, 10 🔎 In short: On six points — the projection’s assumptions, efforts to increase children, the school-route lines, the criteria for Phase 2, consensus-building and the closed buildings — the published materials do not provide what is needed to judge. Six points that could not be confirmed from the published material. The question is not whether the plan is right, but whether the information needed to judge it is there. ① and ④ concern the forecast and the criteria for decisions, ③ and ⑥ the boundary and the buildings, and ② and ⑤ the way the process is run. Some of these questions cannot be answered by the school reorganization office alone. Increasing the number of children (②) and the use of closed schools (⑥) belong to other departments, and partly to prefectural and national rules. The next section sets out who can decide what.
Review: what the plan does not say

1. The assumptions behind “one class per year by 2033” are not shown 【Fact】The city states that “given the decline in the number of children there is no time to spare, and the reorganization must be carried out as soon as possible”, and expects every elementary school in the district and Shinooka Junior High to have one class per year group by 2033. 🔎 Our view: Only the result of the projection has been published. The assumptions behind it — births, families moving in and out, new housing — are not in any published material we could find. If they were shown, residents could tell apart what cannot be changed from what policy could still change.
Review: what the plan does not say

2. Nothing in the plan works on increasing the number of children 【Fact】The published plan is built around reorganizing schools. The national guidance revised in August 2026 sets out a “whole-of-government” pillar, asking that the mayoral departments as well as the board of education consider schools together with transport and town planning. 🔎 Our view: Reorganization responds to the fall in the number of children; responding to the fall itself — housing, childcare, transport — sits with other departments. The published material does not show the two being considered in the same place.
Review: what the plan does not say

3. It is hard to see why the eligibility line falls where it does 【Fact】The school bus covers children who live 2 km or more away, plus areas set with local conditions in mind. However, for Shiroyama 3-chome and 4-chome, children are not covered even if the change of school district takes their journey past 2 km. The city has said the guidelines setting stops, timetables and rules are to be handed out at briefings; applications were accepted from 30 August to 30 September 2026. 🔎 Our view: The same 2 km can mean covered in one case and not covered in another, and the reason is not easy to read out of the published material. The application deadline also falls before the content of the guidelines is settled.
Review: what the plan does not say

4. There is no stated test for moving to Phase 2 【Fact】Phase 2 — merging into one elementary and one junior high school with integrated 9-year education — is to be considered “if the number of children falls further after Phase 1”, with the decision made in the light of how Phase 1 goes. 🔎 Our view: What level “falls further” refers to is not stated. Unless it is said in advance how Phase 1 will be judged, Phase 2 reads as a route already fixed.
Review: what the plan does not say

5. How should the consultation process be judged? 【Fact】The public comment drew 142 submissions from 55 people. In the city assembly’s general questions, the high share of submissions calling for the plan to be reviewed or halted became a point of debate. The revised national guidance newly adds both “careful, dialogue-based discussion” and a timeline that “does not put off reaching a conclusion”. 🔎 Our view: Fifty-five people is not a large number against the population of the district, and the count alone cannot measure support or opposition. What matters is not how many replied but how the process was designed: who was reached, and at which stage anything could still change.
Review: what the plan does not say

6. There is no decided use for the buildings after closure 【Fact】What happens to the closing schools is described in published material as a matter for later consideration. Nationwide, 74.4% of surviving closed-school buildings are in use for something else (MEXT, FY2024 survey). 🔎 Our view: A school is an evacuation site and a place where local events happen. If closure runs ahead of any decision on the buildings, the district is left without that base for a period. The closure dates and the plan for the buildings ought to be shown together.
Who decides, and how far the city’s own powers reach

Who decides, and how far the city’s own powers reach

① Responsibility is split across five departments or more 【Fact】In the published material, school reorganization sits with the School Reorganization Section of the General Affairs Division of Education; development of the east with the Eastern District Development Promotion Office of the Urban Policy Department; housing and land use with the Urban Planning Division of the same department; childcare and marriage support with the Children’s Future Department (Children’s Policy Division, and the Meeting and Marriage Support Office created in FY2023); business location with the Business Location and Next-Generation Industry Division of the Regional Revitalization Department; and overall coordination with the Secretarial and Policy Division of the Mayor’s Office. Budgets and ordinances go through a vote of the city council. 🔎 Our view: No department in that list holds “the number of children in the eastern district” as its own target. The School Reorganization Section responds to the decline; it is not the section that reverses it, and the measures that might are spread across several departments. In FY2023 the city did assemble a cross-departmental team from six offices to work on the declining birthrate. Whether the same can be done for a place — the east — is the crux.
Who decides, and how far the city’s own powers reach

② What lay outside the city’s powers 【Fact】Tokadai New Town was built by Aichi Prefecture as a new residential district development project. The Tokadai Line was not the city’s own undertaking, and closed in 2006 because of poor performance. Class-size standards and teacher allocation follow national and prefectural rules. The line between the urbanization promotion area and the urbanization control area is drawn by the prefecture, and most of the eastern district outside Tokadai New Town is urbanization control area. 🔎 Our view: Many of the big decisions that gave the east its shape were not the city’s to make alone. That is not the same as saying there was nothing the city could do. As the next card shows, the city has a record of overcoming exactly these limits.
Who decides, and how far the city’s own powers reach

③ How the city has overcome the limits of the system — and the tool it has not yet used 【Fact】Where the national waiver of nursery fees starts at age three, the city has waived fees for children aged 0–2 from FY2023 out of its own budget. Mumps vaccination has been free since October 2011, and Komaki is the only city in Aichi to do this. Marriage support is funded through the national grant for priority measures against the declining birthrate. In May 2021 the city was selected as an “SDGs Future City” by the Cabinet Office. Its designated factory sites are covered by the prefecture’s industrial location tax scheme. And both the Tokadai district plan and the location optimization plan are decided by the city itself. 🔎 Our view: There are three ways the city has overcome its limits: ① adding its own top-up to national or prefectural schemes, ② going after national or prefectural grants and designations, and ③ using the planning powers it holds itself. It has a record on ① and ②. It is ③ that is thin. Both the district plan and the location optimization plan are the city’s to decide, yet the housing forms and the guided areas in the east have not moved in response to the district losing more people than any other. The tool that would work best in the east is the one least used.
Review: the reorganization and the quality of education

Part 2 Quality of education Key points 🔎6–8, 💡①–⑤ and ⑪–⑮ 🔎 In short: The city shows “the problems of today’s small schools”, but there is no yardstick yet for checking whether learning and growth improve afterwards. Little has been published on class size, teachers, the transition period, or health and safety. The city gives “a better educational environment for children” as the reason for the reorganization. So how will children's learning and growth actually change? Looking at academic ability (understanding and being able to do), personal strengths (relating to others, taking the initiative, taking on challenges) and the conditions behind both (class size, teachers, the transition period, health and safety), we set out what the published material confirms and what it leaves unclear.
Review: the reorganization and the quality of education

1. The educational reason the city gives is “the problems of small schools” 【Fact】The city's New School Development Plan makes “learning together” — children listening to each other and deepening their learning by accepting each other's ideas — the core of its teaching, and says this calls for groups large enough to meet a range of ways of thinking and values. The city's optimal size is 12–24 classes per school for both elementary and junior high (2–4 classes per grade in elementary, 4–8 in junior high), a different range from the national standard of 12–18. In its responses to the public comments, the city accepts that small schools have the advantage of keeping every child in view, and then lists the problems: fewer chances to meet a variety of people, no class reshuffles so relationships become fixed, fewer chances to push each other to grow, and difficulty securing places to shine such as club activities and committees. 🔎 Our view: What is set out are “the problems of today's small schools”. We found no yardstick in the published material for checking what has improved, and by how much, after the reorganization. Nor do the problems the city lists include whether a junior high can have a specialist teacher for every subject (we take this up in the next section).
Review: the reorganization and the quality of education

2. Academic ability: how will “understanding and being able to do” change? 【Fact】Where the city's material touches on academic ability, it is the advantages of the integrated elementary–junior high education being considered for Phase 2 (systematic learning across nine years, easing the stumble on entering junior high, continuing support suited to each child), and the city's recognition that small classes allow close teaching attuned to each child. One public comment said that the claim that integrated education raises academic ability comes with no supporting evidence. At the parents' briefings, some asked whether, with more children, help for those falling behind would be neglected, and others asked for ordinary lessons rather than inquiry lessons to raise academic ability. 🔎 Our view: The published material says neither where the district's children stand academically now nor what the aim is for after the reorganization. Making a school bigger cannot in general be said to raise academic ability in itself; what matters is how small-group teaching, teaching matched to each child's level, and a system for passing records of where a child struggles on to the next grade and school are put in place.
Review: the reorganization and the quality of education

3. Personal strengths: relating to others, taking the initiative, taking on challenges 【Fact】The city explains that each child's abilities grow and social skills develop when children meet a variety of ways of thinking, accept each other, cooperate and push each other to improve. “Learning together” stresses listening to each other without dismissing the other's ideas, and staying beside a child who doesn't understand and explaining in words that get through. At the same time, the city itself lists as a drawback of integrated elementary–junior high education that older elementary pupils get fewer chances, as the oldest in the school, to develop leadership and independence. Komaki City has made a declaration as a “No. 1 City for Children's Dreams and Challenges”. 🔎 Our view: For personal strengths the reorganization cuts both ways. Children will meet more people and have more activities to choose from, but each child's share of roles — committee member, leading a school event, getting to play in a match — may thin out. The published material does not say how the experience of small schools, where every child had some role, will be kept in a large one. The “leadership of older pupils” problem the city itself raised can also arise simply because schools get bigger.
Review: the reorganization and the quality of education

4. Conditions: class size after the merger depends on the size of the year group 【Fact】The maximum class size (35; in the second and third years of junior high it is being lowered from 40 step by step until FY2027), the prefectural and national moves to lower it, and the city’s answers in the council are summarized under “Learning and support after the reorganization” on the plan overview page. The city added to the plan that “optimal size” means the number of classes, not the number of children per class, and that it has no intention of rejecting small classes. At the briefings, parents spoke of their worry that children used to classes of just over 20 will join classes near the maximum after the reorganization, and asked for smaller classes and assistant homeroom teachers for the first few years. How a year group splits into classes under a cap of 35 (our worked example; actual class formation is decided by the prefecture and the city) Pupils in the year group Classes Pupils per class 30 1 30 36 2 18 70 2 35 71 3 23〜24 🔎 Our view: As the table shows, class size jumps up and down each time a year group crosses 35 or 70. The “about 21–25” given in the council can be met by a year group of 36 or 71, but a year group of 70 ends up in classes of 35. Whether such year groups will get an extra class or extra teachers, and how classes will be formed during the transition, is not in the published material.

5. Conditions: learning and wellbeing during the transition 【Fact】Recognizing that a big change of environment can weigh on children's minds and bodies, the city is running exchanges between schools before the reorganization (in elementary schools, hands-on arts and culture lessons and an exchange event in Tokadai Central Park; in junior high, joint satoyama conservation and arts appreciation by Shinooka and Hikarigaoka Junior High). It also states that it will publicize and strengthen the counseling provided by each school's counselors and school counselors, pass on information and support methods for children who need support, and maintain special-needs classes and resource-room instruction. The city also told the city council that it is considering opening a comprehensive education support center for children not attending school, with closed school buildings as one candidate site (not yet decided; Komaki City Council newsletter). 🔎 Our view: The support arrangements are set out, but we found nothing on how the city will check whether the exchanges are frequent and substantial enough. If Phase 2 goes ahead, some children will see their school environment change twice during compulsory education, and nothing has yet been said about support for them.
Review: the reorganization and the quality of education

6. Conditions: teachers and the content of education decide its quality 【Fact】The city explains that staff numbers will rise as pupil numbers rise with the reorganization, and that it is working with the prefecture so that staff can be placed as planned for FY2027. Under national law (the Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers, Article 7 and others), staff numbers are calculated from the number of classes. Since July 2025 a preparatory research committee has been discussing the new schools' curriculum, educational goals, club activities and so on. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 4). 🔎 Our view: What the arrangement with the prefecture involves (how many more teachers, and in what form) and the new schools' curriculum and educational goals do not appear in writing in the published material we could check.
Review: the reorganization and the quality of education

7. Conditions: health and safety (school health and medical care) 【Fact】As a heatstroke measure, the city says it is installing bottle-refill water dispensers in every elementary and junior high school for use from summer 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 5). The gyms and grounds of closing schools will be kept from FY2027 onward and are expected to remain designated as evacuation shelters and sites. By law, elementary and junior high schools must have a school nurse-teacher (School Education Act, Articles 37 and 49), and the number is calculated as one for every school with three or more classes, plus one more for elementary schools of 801 or more pupils and junior highs of 751 or more (Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers, Article 8). 🔎 Our view: Going from eight schools to four also means going from eight health rooms to four, and each school nurse-teacher will look after more children. We found nothing in the published material on physical fitness now that bus commuting means less daily walking, or on bus travel and admission at the new schools for children who need medical care.

The quality of education is not decided by school size alone. Starting from what the national curriculum asks of each subject, we consider what the reorganization could bring this district's children from eight angles: subject expertise, mathematical ability, the ability to use information, the ability to run a project, the ability to manage a community, and the ability to get through life, everyday life skills and the ability to protect one's health. The 🔎 and 💡 that follow the 【Fact】 are all our own ideas, not something the city is considering. Using information 🔎 Our view: Every school has one device per pupil, so information literacy depends less on school size than on how the devices are used. Running a project 🔎 Our view: The term “project management” does not appear in the Courses of Study, but the cycle in integrated studies and special activities — setting a question, planning, dividing roles, carrying it out and looking back — amounts to it. This ability only grows by actually taking on a role. That large schools tend to leave some children without a role is the same problem as 3 in the previous section.

Managing a community 🔎 Our view: Local studies in social studies and the period for integrated studies are where this is learned. This district faces exactly the problems of community management — a falling population, what to do with closing school buildings, commuting and public transport — and the children are themselves among those affected by the reorganization. At the briefings some asked for inquiry learning such as an elementary school's rapeseed-blossom project to be kept, while others wanted ordinary lessons instead of inquiry, so inquiry needs to be shown to connect with academic ability.

Getting through life 🔎 Our view: This is the ability to protect one's own life and those around one in disasters and extreme heat. The closed schools will remain as shelters, but children will go every day to a different, more distant school. Knowing the shelter near home, and what to do if disaster strikes on the way to or from school or on the bus, needs to be learned both at school and in the community, but we found nothing on this in the published material.

Everyday life skills 🔎 Our view: This is the “ability to run one's own life” that home economics and life environment studies develop. Children who go by bus will need new independence — moving to a timetable, managing their own belongings, letting someone know on days they won't ride. On the other hand, the chances of meeting local people along the walking route may shrink.

Protecting one's health 🔎 Our view: What is learned in health lessons (health, preventing illness, first aid) and the school health system that supports it are two different things. The former depends little on school size; the latter (health rooms, school nurse-teachers, school doctors, medical care) changes with the number and size of schools (7 in the previous section).

Rules for streaming songs (Copyright Act) [Fact] Lyrics and music are copyrighted works, and streaming them online requires the copyright holder’s permission (Copyright Act, Art. 23). Performing them free of charge and not for profit, such as at school events, needs no permission (Art. 38(1)), but this exception does not cover streaming. Singers and performers have performers’ rights (Art. 90-2 onward), and copyright generally lasts until 70 years after the author’s death (Art. 51). When the rights holder cannot be found, a work can be used under a ruling by the Commissioner for Cultural Affairs (Art. 67).

Here are some this site could confirm in posts from the 2026 school year. ・Shinooka Elementary School: its website carries the “Shinooka Karuta”, a set of local karuta cards that turns the area’s history, ways of life and nature into 36 pairs of picture cards and explanation cards. Fifth graders pick grapes with the help of local grape farmers. ・Momogaoka Elementary School: the brass band club takes part in the Citizens’ Festival parade. ・Shinooka Junior High School: ahead of its closure, it has started having students learn the school’s history from the timeline and aerial photos in the principal’s office. ・Toryo Junior High School: students cook with peaches grown in the eastern district by a parent.

A local tradition: Bo-no-te [Fact] The eastern district has two forms of bo-no-te (a traditional staff-fighting performance) designated as intangible folk cultural properties by the city. Okusa Bo-no-te (Shinkage school, designated in 1983) is offered at the festival of Okusa Hachiman Shrine in Okusa, and Noguchi Bo-no-te (Genji Ten school, designated in 1970) at the festival of Noguchi Shinmei Shrine; both are performed every year on the second Sunday of October. Both died out for a time after the war, but local people formed preservation societies, revived them and still pass them on (published by the Komaki City Cultural Properties Division).

Festivals of the east [Fact] Across the eastern district, festivals have gone on apart from the schools. The Tokadai Festival in Tokadai Central Park is a summer event full of bon-odori dancing; its 40th edition was held in July 2026, and the city’s Eastern District Development Office had a booth there (“Eastern District Development News”). Shinooka Elementary’s “Shinooka Karuta” introduces the festival music and mikomai dance kept up by a preservation society at the Ikenouchi festival, and the fire-walking ritual at Fukugonji Temple in Okusa. Local specialties of the east [Fact] The city presents Nagoya Cochin chicken as a specialty of the eastern district, and local groups have held cooking sessions in Toryo Junior High’s cooking room making hikizuri-nabe, a local Nagoya Cochin dish, and dishes using grapes (published by the Eastern District Development Office). Ancient kilns and the history of pottery [Fact] From the 7th to the 11th century, the Shinooka district was, together with the Sanage kilns, a center of pottery making (ceramics) in the Owari region. More than 110 kiln sites have been found, known as the Shinooka Ancient Kiln Sites. They were half-underground “ana-gama” tunnel kilns, dug as narrow trenches into hill slopes and roofed with clay; Sue ware was fired in the 7th–8th centuries and ash-glazed ware from the late 9th century. Characters written on Sue ware from Shinooka Kiln No. 78 closely resemble those on Sue ware found at the Fujiwara capital in Nara, showing that Shinooka’s vessels travelled as far as Nara. The exhibition design (March 2025) for the city’s Komaki History Discovery Museum (こまき歴史発見館), now open on the 4th floor of Lapio with free admission, also planned a corner on the Shinooka kilns where visitors can touch pottery shards.
Proposal: carrying on our schools’ legacy

Oyama Temple Ruins and Chigo Shrine [Fact] In Oyama are the ruins of Oyamamine Shofukuji, a temple thought to have been founded in the late 7th century: the “Oyama Temple Ruins”. It once flourished so much that people said “Enryakuji on Mt. Hiei in the west, Oyama Temple in the east”, but it was burned in an attack in the mid-12th century. It is a national historic site — one of only two in the city, with Komakiyama. Chigo Shrine to its south is said to have been built to console the spirits of two temple boys who died in the attack, and its approach, lined with nearly 100 cherry trees, is a well-known cherry-blossom spot. The exhibition design (March 2025) for the city’s Komaki History Discovery Museum (こまき歴史発見館), now open on the 4th floor of Lapio with free admission, planned a corner on the ruins showing the pagoda’s foundation stones life-size on the floor.

Part 3 The number of children Key points 🔎9, 💡⑥–⑩ 🔎 In short: Factory attraction and industrial estates added jobs, but not children. What did not work was child-rearing support that is the same across the city; what was missing was the right types of housing and transport. 【Fact】Jobs in the east (2009 → 2014) Establishments 917 → 1,095 Employees 12,388 → 20,671 【Fact】Children in the east Under-20s: less than half of 20 years ago Population peaked at 39,350 in 2004 What worked Industrial estates and new businesses added jobs. What did not work Child-rearing support that is the same across the city does not close the gap between districts. What was missing Housing young households can move into, and ways to commute. The number of children fell, but not because nothing was done here. Over recent decades the city has courted factories, built a new town, expanded childcare support, launched a district development strategy and set up marriage support. Following that record through published material, we ask what worked and what did not, judged on one thing only: the number of children in the eastern district. Review: Did past policies reach the east?

① Jobs grew. Children did not 【Fact】Establishments in the eastern district rose from 917 in 2009 to 1,095 in 2014, and employees from 12,388 to 20,671. Over the same period the city as a whole fell from 6,970 to 6,654 establishments and from 103,591 to 100,228 employees (Komaki City, Eastern District Development Strategy). Across the city, 29,416 more people commute in than out, about 55% of them into secondary industry (2020, Komaki City industry status report). 🔎 Our view: The eastern district has succeeded at creating places to work. What did not grow is the district being chosen as a place to live by the people who work there. The question is not how many jobs, but what kind of jobs, and whether the people doing them want to live here.
Review: Did past policies reach the east?

② Citywide childcare support does not close the gap between districts 【Fact】In 2015 the city declared itself a “No.1 City for Children’s Dreams and Challenges”, and from FY2023 it has waived nursery fees for children aged 0–2 out of its own budget. Yet with 2010 set at 100, district populations in 2018 stood at 106.04 for Komaki-minami and 102.90 for Ajioka, against 88.33 for Shinooka (85.42 for Tokadai). Shinooka’s ageing rate also rose from 15.7% in 2010 to 27.3% in 2018 (Komaki City population vision). 🔎 Our view: These measures apply equally wherever you live in the city. So they may affect whether a family chooses Komaki, but they barely affect which district inside Komaki it chooses. That only the east fell so far suggests the reason was not the cost of raising children.
Review: Did past policies reach the east?

③ There was essentially only one kind of housing on offer 【Fact】The Tokadai district plan (adopted 19 September 1989, about 322.2 ha) restricts Zone A, which covers most of the area (about 187.9 ha), to detached single-family houses, with a minimum plot of 150 m² and a height limit of 10 m. Zone B, where mid- and high-rise housing is allowed, is about 4.6 ha (Komaki City urban planning). The Eastern District Development Strategy likewise says that “while roads, parks and other infrastructure are well provided, land use in the residential area is restricted.” The east (Shinooka) has 166 vacant buildings, the most in the city. 🔎 Our view: In an estate everyone moves into at once, the children’s generation moves out twenty to thirty years later. For young households to move in at that point, another kind of housing is needed — homes to rent, smaller units, apartments. That the district has the most vacant houses in the city and still no young households is, we think, not because there are too few houses but because there are too few houses of a kind they can move into.
Review: Did past policies reach the east?

④ The city’s own survey puts transport, not childcare, at the top of the reasons for leaving 【Fact】In the city’s 2018 survey of people moving in and out, people in their 20s to 40s who moved to neighboring municipalities most often chose their destination because “commuting to work or school is easy” and “public transport is convenient”. What they had been unhappy about in Komaki was, again at the top, “public transport is inconvenient” and “there is a lot of congestion”. Nobody chose “the education environment is good” as a reason for their destination, and nobody named “childcare support” as a source of dissatisfaction with Komaki (Komaki City population vision). 🔎 Our view: The city’s own survey says young households leave over transport, not childcare support. The eastern district lost that transport in 2006 — two years after its population peaked in 2004. We cannot establish cause and effect, but the order of events cannot be ignored.
Review: Did past policies reach the east?

⑤ Work on marriage and singlehood only began in FY2023 【Fact】The city’s own analysis found that the indicator most strongly correlated with the total fertility rate is the proportion of unmarried women, where Komaki ranks 30th of the 38 cities in Aichi; it ranks 35th for the share of men in regular employment and 32nd for the marital fertility rate. The “Meeting and Marriage Support Office” was created in FY2023, and the contracted marriage support program and matchmaking subsidy began in FY2024 (Komaki City analysis of declining birthrate). 🔎 Our view: Marriage is the entrance to the birth figures. The dedicated office was created nineteen years after the eastern district’s population peaked, and results there would take another decade or more to show up as pupils in a school. It is not a measure that can arrive in time for the first phase of the reorganization in FY2027.
Review: Did past policies reach the east?

⑥ Two plans for the same district rest on opposite assumptions 【Fact】The KPI of the Eastern District Development Strategy (FY2022–2031) is the working-age share of the population: the target is to raise the projected 53.0% by one point by FY2026, and the projected 48.7% by two points by FY2031. The school reorganization plan, meanwhile, takes as its premise that by 2033 every elementary school in the district and Shinooka Junior High will have one class per year group. 🔎 Our view: The development plan sets out to move the population structure; the school plan assumes the population will not move. Both are the city’s own plans, for the same district. We could not find, in the published material, any sign that the two have been set against each other in the same forum.
Review: what the prefecture and the state have done

🔎 In short: The prefecture built the new town and its transport. National birth-rate measures and regional revitalization have not changed the trend. The state is making classes smaller while merging schools, but only the latter affects this district. City policy is not the only thing that has moved the population of the eastern district. The new town, and its transport, were both prefectural undertakings, and the wider framework for the falling birthrate is set by the state. Here we look at prefectural and national policy through the same single lens: the number of children in the eastern district.
Review: what the prefecture and the state have done

① National policy on the birthrate has not stopped the fall in births 【Fact】In October 2019 the state made early childhood education and care free (for ages 3–5, and for ages 0–2 in households exempt from residence tax); in April 2023 it created the Children and Families Agency; and in December of that year the Cabinet adopted the “Children’s Future Strategy”, whose “Acceleration Plan” makes FY2024–2026 an intensive period. From October 2024 the income cap on the child allowance was abolished and payment extended to high-school age. Yet in 2024 there were 686,061 births — the first time the figure has fallen below 700,000 since records began in 1899 — and the total fertility rate was 1.15, the lowest ever (Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, vital statistics). 🔎 Our view: These measures matter as ways of easing the burden on households that already have children. But easing that burden has not reversed the fall in births itself. It is the same shape as Komaki’s childcare support failing to bring children back to the east.
Review: what the prefecture and the state have done

② Regional revitalization did not change where people move 【Fact】In 2014 the state enacted the Regional Revitalization Act, setting a target of zero net in-migration to the Tokyo area by 2020. In the government’s own ten-year review, published in 2024, it was accepted that the broad trends of population decline and concentration in the Tokyo area could not be changed. Komaki drew up its population vision and comprehensive strategy under that framework in FY2015, and a second edition in FY2019. 🔎 Our view: Regional revitalization asked every municipality to write a plan, but what decides where people live is work, transport and housing. In the eastern district, as the city’s own survey shows, the reasons for leaving were commuting and public transport. A requirement to write plans did not move any of those three.
Review: what the prefecture and the state have done

③ The prefecture is the party that built the east’s housing and its transport 【Fact】Tokadai New Town was built by Aichi Prefecture as a new residential district development project, and people began moving in in 1980. The Tokadai Line closed in 2006 because of poor performance. The line between the urbanization promotion area and the urbanization control area is also drawn by the prefecture. As birthrate policy the prefecture has adopted the “Aichi Hagumin Plan” and runs a matchmaking support portal, “Aicon Navi”, for people who wish to marry. The city’s designated factory sites are covered by the prefecture’s industrial location tax scheme. 🔎 Our view: Ranked by effect, what the prefecture has done to the east is: it built the housing estate, its transport was lost, and it encouraged factories to locate there. Both the prefecture and the city offer childcare and marriage support, but it was the first three that actually moved the population.
Review: what the prefecture and the state have done

4. The state is lowering the class-size cap while also encouraging school mergers 【Fact】In 2021 the state amended the class-size law, lowering the cap for public elementary schools from 40 to 35 over five years. At the same time the standard school size remains 12 to 18 classes, and the guidance revised in August 2026 is built on wider areas, integration and modernization (Nationwide). A further amendment in March 2026 (Act No. 7 of 2026) set the junior high maximum at 35 as well, lowering it grade by grade until FY2027. 🔎 Our view: Lowering the cap adds classes and makes them smaller at schools with large year groups. At schools where a year group is under 35, numbers are already below the cap, so nothing changes. The city expects every elementary school in the district to have one class per year group by 2033. At such schools the lower cap does nothing; the policy actually at work here is the one that merges schools. The lower cap only starts to matter once merging has made year groups larger.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

💡 In short: Ten proposals, on housing types, transport, settlement support, entry points for work and responsible departments, so that past oversights are not repeated. Proposals meant to keep the same oversights from being repeated when the second phase is judged and the closed school buildings are given a use. The city is not considering them.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

1. The mix of housing types should have been kept open The thinking: A district plan of detached houses only, on plots of 150 m² or more, assumes the generation that moved in will simply grow old there. The turnover that inevitably arrives twenty to thirty years after occupation should have been anticipated, with room left for rentable homes and smaller units. What can be done now: the district plan is the city’s to decide. Alongside a way of turning the city’s largest stock of vacant buildings — 166 in the east — into homes young families can move into (renovation support, leasing, splitting into two-household homes), there is room to revisit the rules on use and plot size.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

2. When the transport link was lost, housing policy should have been adjusted with it The thinking: The closure of the Tokadai Line in 2006 changed the premise of the eastern housing estates. As the city’s own survey shows, young households pick their destination first on commuting and public transport. At the moment of closure, the standard of replacement transport should have been fixed as a condition of housing policy. What can be done now: handle the school bus in the same forum as adults’ commuting. The revised national guidance likewise asks municipalities to secure transport for the area as a whole, in cooperation with the mayor’s side of the administration.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

3. Settlement support should have been weighted towards the district losing the most people The thinking: The settlement subsidy and grant apply to the whole city, and as far as we could confirm nothing is weighted towards the east. With Shinooka at 88.33 and Tokadai at 85.42 against 2010, spreading the same money evenly cannot close that gap. What can be done now: add a top-up for the east. The location optimization plan already designates the area around Tokadai Center as a “local hub”, and it is the city that decides how each area is treated.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

4. The door to business attraction should have been opened beyond factories and logistics The thinking: The city’s business location subsidy requires a new or expanded factory of 1,000 m² or more and fixed-asset spending of ¥500 million or more (¥100 million for small and medium enterprises). The five designated factory sites are for factories too. By the city’s own analysis, its industrial structure has an extremely high share of “manufacturing” and “transport and postal services”, while employees per establishment in “information and communications” are considerably below average. Work in IT, design, apparel, music, film and culture reaches neither that floor area nor that level of capital spending. Structurally, there was never a route for such businesses into this district. What can be done now: create a small-scale category measured by people employed and by the business continuing, rather than by floor area and capital spending. The city’s next-generation industry subsidies do include information and communications, but they are for equipment bought by existing small and medium firms in the city — they do not reach small businesses arriving from outside, or people starting out.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

5. A town people commute into has to be turned into a town people want to live in The thinking: 29,416 more people commute in than out, while the age groups that start families show a net outflow. Work here, live elsewhere: that state of affairs has lasted a long time. Living close to work ought to be this district’s strength, and the Eastern District Development Strategy itself calls for “an environment that makes working from home easier”. What can be done now: put workplaces — coworking, satellite offices — into vacant houses and shops in the east, and make them the landing place for the settlement grant’s “new life support for people working in the city”. The scheme already exists; what is missing is somewhere in the east for it to land.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

6. The district should have kept a place where cultural and creative work can grow The thinking: Work in apparel, design, music and film needs neither large floors nor expensive equipment, but it does need cheap workspace and somewhere people gather. The east has peach and grape growing, the Shiki-no-Mori park, 32 parks in all — and eight school buildings about to fall empty. Nationally, 74.4% of surviving closed school buildings are in use for something else (Nationwide). What can be done now: when the use of the closing buildings is decided, put workshops, studios and rehearsal rooms on the list of options from the start. Work that combines local produce with design fits the strategy’s own aim of “creating new appeal from local resources”, and children seeing real work close at hand fits its aim of “an environment in which young people grow attached to the eastern district”.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

7. “The number of children in the east” should have been some department’s target The thinking: In FY2023 the city assembled a cross-departmental team from six offices to work on the declining birthrate. Nothing of the kind exists for the east as a place. The Eastern District Development Strategy’s KPI is the working-age share of the population, not the number of children. What can be done now: put the Eastern District Development Council and the school reorganization review on the same agenda, and adopt the district’s child population as a shared indicator. Then decide which department answers for that figure.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

8. Bundle national and prefectural schemes onto one place: the east The thinking: The city has a record of going out and getting things — topping up nursery fees, free vaccination, marriage support funded by a national grant, selection as a Cabinet Office “SDGs Future City”, designation under the prefecture’s industrial location tax scheme. But most of it is aimed at the whole city, and none of it is bundled onto the district losing the most people. What can be done now: layer the housing, transport, work and childcare schemes onto one place. The same money, narrowed to one district, might be enough to change a decision about where to live.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

9. The prefecture and the city need a way of seeing an estate through its turnover of generations The thinking: Aichi Prefecture built Tokadai New Town; Komaki built and has maintained the schools in it. When, forty years after occupation, the children were gone, the clearing-up appeared as the city’s school reorganization. We found no mechanism by which the body that builds a town stays with it for a full cycle. What can be done now: put the renewal of a prefecture-built estate — revisiting permitted uses, supporting people to move house, getting vacant homes onto the market — onto the same table as the city’s Eastern District Development Strategy, and negotiate it with the prefecture. Pulling prefectural schemes into the east is an extension of exactly what the city has already done with grants and designations.
What should have been done, and what can be done now

10. Uniform national support needed a way of choosing a place The thinking: Free early childhood education and the expanded child allowance are available identically anywhere in Japan. So they bear neither on “where in Japan to live” nor on “where in the city to live”. To make them bite in the district losing the most people, something has to be able to choose a place. What can be done now: when the city uses a national or prefectural grant, it can apply with a narrowed target area. It has already done this with the national birthrate grant for marriage support; the same approach could be extended to housing, transport and work.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

💡 In short: Seven proposals for increasing the number of children in the whole district, separate from where the schools go. Separately from how schools are arranged, what would it take to increase the number of children in the Shinooka district itself? Everything below is this site’s own proposal; none of it is under consideration by the city.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

1. Publish the assumptions and a target Nobody can work out how much of what would change the outlook without knowing the assumptions behind the projection. If they were published, residents, businesses and the city could argue on the same numbers.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

2. Help Tokadai New Town turn over to a new generation While the under-19 population has halved, the over-65 population has grown about 2.5 times. In a neighborhood settled all at once, room for families with children appears as people move on. Tracking empty homes and helping families move into them needs no change to where schools are.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

3. Treat the commute as a condition for settling here On school buses, the revised national guidance notes the shortage of drivers and states that it matters to work with the mayoral departments to secure transport for the area as a whole. A child’s school bus and an adult’s commute are two sides of one problem. How easy it is to reach Kasugai — the Tokadai–Torimatsu road and the bus services — bears directly on whether families with children choose this district.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

4. Make the schools themselves a reason to choose the area The national guidance says that where schools stay small, as much as where they merge, work is needed to draw on the advantages and keep the drawbacks small. Nationwide there are now 232 public compulsory education schools covering all nine years (75,828 pupils, FY2024). The integrated 9-year education being considered for Phase 2 could instead be designed up front as the district’s own character, rather than arriving as a by-product of merging.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

5. Use a closing school as a base for families Nationwide, 74.4% of surviving closed-school buildings are in use. If one of the eight closing schools near the center of the district were given over to childcare support, after-school space and community meeting rooms, it would partly make up for the greater distances that merging brings.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

6. Put the board of education and the mayoral departments in the same room None of items 1–5 can be decided by the board of education alone. The “whole-of-government” pillar of the revised national guidance asks for exactly this: considering schools as a question about the area’s future. Simply adding the housing, transport and childcare departments to the reorganization discussions would widen what can be discussed.
Ideas: how to increase the number of children

7. Examine whether a high school could be placed in this district There is no high school here; children can stay inside the district up to junior high, but not after that, and the district has lost its university too. While the use of the closing school sites is still open, placing a high school there (including a combined junior and senior high school) can still be considered. The next section sets this out in full.
Could a high school fit in this district?

💡 In short: There is no high school in this district. With five facts and three proposals, we look at keeping a high school as an option before the use of the school sites is decided. Phase 2 is about joining elementary and junior high education, but this district has no high school at all. The time when the use of the closing school sites is decided is also the last time this question can be asked. This section does not claim that building a high school would increase the number of children. With a university leaving the district and prefectural high schools being consolidated, putting a high school here runs against the current. Even so, once the use of the sites is settled the option disappears altogether — which is why it deserves to be examined once, before that decision. To the questions → ↑ Back to the key points
Could a high school fit in this district?

① There is no high school in the district 【Fact】Komaki has four high schools: the prefectural Komaki (Komaki 1-chome), Komaki Minami (Ogihigashi) and Komaki Kouka (Kuboisshiki), and the private Homare (Honjo). All of them lie outside the Shinooka district (city facility guide). There is no high school inside the district. 🔎 Our view: Up to junior high, children can reach school inside the district; after that they travel out of it. One public comment said the area suits families raising children but becomes inconvenient from high school onwards. When a family asks how long it can stay here, that step counts.
Could a high school fit in this district?

② Universities and high schools are leaving this area 【Fact】Nagoya University of the Arts moved from Okusa in Komaki to the city of Nagoya in April 2022. At a town meeting held at the Eastern Citizens' Center, the city explained that universities across the country are returning to city centers, moving to well-connected places where students are easier to attract in a time of fewer children; it added that the vacated land belongs to the university, so the city cannot decide its use, but that it strongly hopes for a good one. Aichi Bunkyo University, also in Okusa, has announced that it will stop admitting students from FY2027 (decided at an extraordinary board meeting on 30 March 2026), citing the falling 18-year-old population and years of enrollment below capacity, and says it will provide its teaching and research environment until the current students graduate.Homare High School (Honjo), the city's private high school, has announced on its own site (3 June 2026) that it will move to Minato ward in Nagoya in 2029. The destination is reported to be the site of the former Nagoya racecourse. 🔎 Our view: Before this district can ask whether it could host a high school, it is already losing the places of learning it has. The reasons the universities gave — fewer 18-year-olds, and location — are exactly the conditions any school placed here would run into. So the proposals below are not “invite a school and people will come back”; they are “take these conditions into account when the use of the school sites is decided”.The private high school's move points the same way: schools are gathering where the people are.
Could a high school fit in this district?

③ The moment to decide what the sites are for is now 【Fact】The city says that unless there is a plan to convert a closed school building — one worth its considerable upkeep — the building will in principle be demolished, to hold down costs. Gymnasiums and grounds are to be kept as bases for local sport and disaster response, and the use of the sites is under study by the relevant departments (the city's replies to the public comment and at the parents' briefings). The city also lists Shinooka Elementary among five schools over 60 years old for which a decision must be made soon (New School Development Plan). 🔎 Our view: “Demolition unless there is a plan to convert” means the window for putting a plan forward is limited. Shinooka Elementary and Shinooka Junior High stand where the district's original one-elementary-one-junior-high pair was, but given their age this is a question about the land, not about reusing the present buildings.
Could a high school fit in this district?

④ Three legal forms exist, and one works across different founders 【Fact】Integrated junior/senior high education takes three forms: the secondary school, the attached type in which one founder links a junior high and a high school, and the co-operative type, which works even when the founders differ (School Education Act art. 71; its Enforcement Regulation arts. 75 and 87). In the co-operative type the founder of the junior high agrees the curriculum with the founder of the high school. A municipality establishing a high school or a secondary school needs the approval of the prefectural board of education (School Education Act art. 4), and the prefecture pays staff salaries only up to the lower division of a secondary school (Act on the Salary Burden for Municipal School Staff art. 1). 🔎 Our view: A high school run by the city alone is heavy on both approval and money. The co-operative type, by contrast, can start without a new building, pairing the reorganized junior highs with a prefectural high school in the city. It can be examined before any attempt to attract a school.
Could a high school fit in this district?

⑤ The prefecture is not adding schools — but it has opened a table 【Fact】All ten prefectural integrated schools Aichi has opened are new junior highs attached to existing prefectural high schools; not one is a newly built school. At the same time the prefecture is consolidating its high schools, with junior high graduates expected to fall by about 20% by FY2035; in FY2028 four schools in the Seto area become three. Its Prefectural High School Reorganization Vision states that a forum will be set up for the prefecture and the municipalities to discuss the future of high schools. 🔎 Our view: The prefecture's own documents make plain that asking for a brand-new high school is unlikely to succeed right now. But since the vision itself provides for a forum, there is a way in for telling the prefecture that this district has no high school at all.
Could a high school fit in this district?

Proposal 1: Put a high school on the list before deciding the sites Once demolition is decided, this can no longer be examined. Simply listing “a high school (including a combined junior–senior high school)” among the options for the sites, and costing it once, changes what the decision rests on.
Could a high school fit in this district?

Proposal 2: Ask the prefecture for the discussion table Where high schools go is the prefecture's decision. Its vision provides for a forum with the municipalities; setting out that this district has no high school, that it is losing its university, and where its children go after junior high could put the question on that agenda.
Could a high school fit in this district?

Proposal 3: The co-operative type is the quickest to start The co-operative type needs no new building: the reorganized Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi junior highs could begin by linking their curriculum with a prefectural high school in the city. The prefecture already has such pairings, and in April 2026 a prefectural high school working with municipal junior highs joined them. If it works, it is a foothold for whatever comes next.

What if my child misses the bus?

If a child misses the bus, the app sends a notice and the school also gets in touch; as a rule the family is asked to handle it. The city says the bus cannot turn back, because that would upset the timetable. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
What happens during typhoons or weather warnings?
What happens when a weather warning is issued will be set out in the “School Bus Use Guidelines”. It is expected to follow the school’s own decision on whether to open.
Can children outside the service area ride the bus?

Eligibility is decided by home address. The city says the covered area has been stretched as far as the bus capacity allows, and children outside it are asked to walk. Where a child cannot walk because of a disability or similar, the city will consider the case individually with the school and the operator. Where the bus leaves a walking group too small, groups will be merged with neighboring ones. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Yes. The city covers all costs because the reorganization increases commute distances for these students. There is no charge for students or families.
Where will the bus stops be?

The city designates the stops. They were chosen mainly on public land, with the safety of waiting children first and with account taken of where children live. Children are expected to walk to the stop as a group, using the existing walking groups. The exact stops and timetable are to be given at the briefings for eligible families. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
When and how do we apply?

In August 2026 the application form and a briefing invitation were posted to guardians of children inside the service area. Forms were accepted from 30 August to 30 September, and the form had to be returned whether or not a seat was wanted. Applications closed on 30 September. See how to apply.
How many runs a day, and how long is the ride?

There is one run in the morning and up to three in the afternoon (after period 5, after period 6, and after club activities). A ride is expected to take at most about 20 minutes, and even the earliest meeting time is to be kept no earlier than 7:20. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Is an adult on board with the children?

Yes, an attendant rides along. The city says it had not planned one at first, but added the role after hearing worries about a child being alone with the driver and requests for help boarding. The attendant helps children on and off, watches over the cabin and responds in emergencies; the role will be filled through an outside contract. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Can parents check that their child got on the bus?

The plan now includes a boarding-check system that lets parents and the school confirm the child got on safely, plus a system to prevent a child being left on board. The city is looking at an ICT-based checking tool and says it will inform parents once the details are fixed. (City's reply in the public comment results) Later, at the June 2026 briefings, the city explained that the bus attendant operates a boarding-check app used with boarding cards, and that parents are notified through the app if a child misses the bus.
How were the bus stop locations decided?

Stops were chosen mainly on public land, putting the safety of waiting children first and taking account of where the children live. As a result, the city says, some stops ended up near the edge of the covered area. Children are expected to walk to the stop as a group, using the existing walking groups. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Will the bus stops have a sign?

No. The city says it will not put up signs, for crime-prevention reasons: marking a spot as a stop would let outsiders know that children gather there at set times. The city assigns each household the stop it will use. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Do children wear seat belts? Where do their school bags go?

The city says children will be told to wear their seat belts. The buses will basically be microbuses with no special space for luggage, so randoseru backpacks and other bags go on the child's lap or under the seat. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Is there a subsidy for electric-assist bicycles? Can children take the Komakuru community bus to school?

Electric-assist bicycles: The city says it is not currently considering a purchase subsidy to encourage commuting by electric-assist bicycle. Komakuru: Komaki's community bus “Komakuru” runs mainly to serve areas with little public transport and to help people reach public facilities, and anyone may ride it. But if it were run on the assumption that students commute on it, it could fill up with children at school times and leave no room for other passengers. The city therefore says it will decide carefully, after talks with the departments concerned, in which cases it can be used for commuting. (The city's responses to the public comments, Nov–Dec 2025)
Can enough bus drivers be found? Who will drive the buses?

Finding drivers: Driver shortages are a problem across Japan, but the city says that school bus work, which unlike route buses rarely involves long shifts, is comparatively easy to staff. Who drives: The school buses are run under contract. When hiring drivers, the contractor checks their years of driving experience and accident record, and manages driving skills, health and the operating system as a whole, including yearly health checks. The city says it will also set up its own checks to keep the service safe. (City's replies at the June 2026 briefings)
Do parents have to take their child to the bus stop every day?

The city says it will not require families to take children to the stop every day. For the children’s safety, it asks families to help with watching over them or taking them when they can, depending on their circumstances. Children are expected to go to the stop together with their current walking group. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)

Moving Club Activities into the Community

A nationwide effort to move club activities, long run by teachers, over to community clubs and organizations. In the Shinooka district this happens at the same time as the school reorganization, so this page shows both together. What the national government has set out: On 22 December 2025 the Japan Sports Agency and MEXT adopted the “Comprehensive Guidelines on Club Activity Reform and the Promotion of Community Club Activities”, under which a “reform implementation period” begins in FY2026. Club activities have until now been run inside schools. With fewer children making clubs hard to sustain, and with the load on teachers, the direction set out is to shift weekend activities step by step to community clubs. In the Shinooka district the schools are to be reorganized in FY2027. What happens to club activities afterwards, and how far community clubs will take them on, has not been announced. The community clubs listed here have not been designated to take over any club activity. The city lists, among the problems of small schools, the difficulty of securing places for children to shine, such as club activities and committees. In the parents' survey (July 2025, 471 responses), the top hope for the reorganization was “more choice of clubs” (55.2%). The new schools' club activities are being discussed by the preparatory research committee, and their types and number will be decided during preparations depending on teacher staffing and facilities after the reorganization. 🏘️ Definition & Purpose A Community Council is an organization voluntarily formed by local residents based on the elementary school district. Groups such as neighborhood associations, PTAs, senior clubs, sports clubs, and welfare commissioners participate across organizational lines to discuss local issues and revitalize community life. In Komaki City, Community Councils have been established in 14 of the city's 16 elementary school districts (as of April 2026). The five elementary school districts in the Shinooka area (Shinooka, Hikarigaoka, Oshiro, Momogaoka, and Sue) each have their own council. 📋 The five Community Councils of the Shinooka area All five elementary school districts in the Shinooka area have a Community Council, and all five were certified by the city on April 1, 2020. The oldest, Sue Elementary District, was founded in 2014 and has over a decade of activity behind it. 🏫 School District as Organizational Base As the name "○○ Elementary School District" implies, the elementary school district is the geographic foundation of each Community Council. School districts serve as units of social cohesion, and Community Councils use this framework to cultivate horizontal connections among residents. 🤝 Community School (School Management Council) Each school in Komaki City has a School Management Council (Community School). This is a forum where parents and local residents can share opinions on the school's educational policies and operations — an important institution connecting Community Councils with schools. It creates opportunities for local adults to participate in classroom support, read-alouds, and career education, and to share school challenges with the wider community. 🏟️ Community Use of School Facilities The gymnasiums, sports fields, and pools of each school are used daily by local residents for community sports and as disaster bases (evacuation sites). Community members also participate in school events such as sports meets and learning fairs, making schools serve as the public "face" of the community. 🎒 After-School Childcare Clubs After-school childcare clubs for children of dual-income families are also organized on a school-district basis and operate in coordination with Community Councils and PTAs. After the reorganization, a club is to be set up inside each of Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi elementary schools (FAQ).
