What will happen to current activities when the councils are reduced to two? The city has announced a policy of reorganizing to 2 Community Councils by FY2029, but how the integration proceeds and how each event will be handled will be determined through consultations with residents and the individual councils. At this point, many details about how activities will be handed over remain undecided, and it is hoped that a forum will be provided for residents' voices to be reflected. Won't community bonds weaken if the local school disappears? Schools have served as hubs for community events, disaster preparedness, sports, and childcare. School consolidation means the number of these hubs will change, but the city has declared a policy of continuing community use of closed school facilities, so gymnasiums and sports fields are expected to remain available. How to rebuild the community itself will need to be discussed with residents taking the lead. Will Community School activities disappear with the school consolidation? They won't disappear. New School Management Councils (Community Schools) will be organized in each of the 4 new schools after reorganization (Tokadai Higashi Elementary, Tokadai Nishi Elementary, Tokadai Higashi Junior High, Tokadai Nishi Junior High). However, how to carry on the relationships and activities cultivated by each current school's Community School depends on future consultations. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026 (“Shinooka School Reorganization News” No. 4). What will happen to local events that each community has independently continued? Events that each Community Council has organized over many years (disaster drills, children's events, local festivals, etc.) are activities carried out by local residents. Even after the councils are integrated, continuation is possible based on the will and consensus of local residents, but the specific form will be at the discretion of the new post-reorganization councils. No official policy has yet been announced.

※ This section summarizes points commonly raised when community organizations based on school districts are merged. How it will actually proceed in the Shinooka district will be decided through discussions between the city and each council. Schools and community ties Schools bring together not only children but also parents and local residents. Events such as sports days, school presentations and evacuation drills are also occasions for people of different generations to meet. For this reason, school mergers are often described as affecting not only the learning environment but also how local people are connected. Points raised when organizations cover a wider area A wider area can make it easier to pool people and funds, and lets residents across a larger area work together. On the other hand, taking part can become harder once activities go beyond the circle of people who know each other, and attachment to the former school district may fade. Which side comes out stronger is generally said to depend on how the transition is handled and how residents take part. How the transition proceeds When local organizations merge, the timing, how activities are handed over, and how residents are informed and consulted become the main issues. In the Shinooka district, the five councils are to be reorganized into two, targeting fiscal 2029, and how the merger proceeds will be decided through future discussions. At the 2025 briefings and public comment process, residents also voiced concern about the future of the local community. Oyama Temple Ruins and Chigo Shrine

In Oyama are the ruins of Oyamamine Shofukuji, a temple thought to have been founded in the late 7th century: the “Oyama Temple Ruins”. It once flourished so much that people said “Enryakuji on Mt. Hiei in the west, Oyama Temple in the east”, but it was burned in an attack in the mid-12th century. It is a national historic site — one of only two in the city, with Komakiyama. Chigo Shrine to its south is said to have been built to console the spirits of two temple boys who died in the attack, and its approach, lined with nearly 100 cherry trees, is a well-known cherry-blossom spot. The exhibition design (March 2025) for the city’s Komaki History Discovery Museum (こまき歴史発見館), now open on the 4th floor of Lapio with free admission, planned a corner on the ruins showing the pagoda’s foundation stones life-size on the floor.
Ancient kilns and the history of pottery

From the 7th to the 11th century, the Shinooka district was, together with the Sanage kilns, a center of pottery making (ceramics) in the Owari region. More than 110 kiln sites have been found, known as the Shinooka Ancient Kiln Sites. They were half-underground “ana-gama” tunnel kilns, dug as narrow trenches into hill slopes and roofed with clay; Sue ware was fired in the 7th–8th centuries and ash-glazed ware from the late 9th century. Characters written on Sue ware from Shinooka Kiln No. 78 closely resemble those on Sue ware found at the Fujiwara capital in Nara, showing that Shinooka’s vessels travelled as far as Nara. The exhibition design (March 2025) for the city’s Komaki History Discovery Museum (こまき歴史発見館), now open on the 4th floor of Lapio with free admission, also planned a corner on the Shinooka kilns where visitors can touch pottery shards.

“Peachliner” was the nickname of the Tokadai Line, a new transit system that linked Tokadai New Town with Meitetsu Komaki Station. It opened on 25 March 1991 and ran 7.4 km on an elevated track from Komaki Station to Tokadai Higashi Station. All seven stations had platform screen doors, and only Komaki and Tokadai Center stations were staffed. Because the new town’s population grew less than expected, among other reasons, it kept losing money and was closed after its last day of service on 30 September 2006. Since that same September, the “Peach Bus” has run between Tokadai and Komaki Station in its place. Aichi Prefecture decided to remove the whole elevated line, and the removal has been carried out step by step. The former depot site in Hikarigaoka 6-chome became land owned jointly by the prefecture and the city, and part of it is used for parking and a pick-up and drop-off loop.

A park of about 6.4 ha in Shiroyama 2-chome, opened in April 1992. It has a wide lawn and a fountain, a long roller slide, an adventure playground and a suspension bridge, and a walking trail through nature on its 100-meter hill. An open-air stage was added in 2002, and the summer Tokadai Festival is held here. The city says it plans to hold exchange events between elementary schools in this park, so that children get used to their new surroundings before the reorganization.

Tokadai New Town is a residential town that Aichi Prefecture built on about 322 ha of hills, and greenways (footpaths) run across it in every direction. This townscape has been chosen by the prefecture as a “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resource”. Tokadai Parks No. 1 to No. 4 (about 2.0–2.7 ha each) are in Shiroyama, Momogaoka, Shinooka and Hikarigaoka, and Tokadai Nishi Park (about 4.15 ha) in Koga opened in 1980, the year residents began moving in. The parks and greenways have wisteria trellises and cherry trees. After the reorganization more children will walk to school along the greenways, and at briefings people have asked for more watching over them there.

A tradition of offering old martial-art forms with staffs and other tools at shrine festivals. Okusa Bo-no-te (Shinkage school) is offered at the festival of Okusa Hachiman Shrine and Noguchi Bo-no-te (Genji Ten school) at that of Noguchi Shinmei Shrine, both every year on the second Sunday of October. Both are intangible folk cultural properties designated by the city. They died out for a time after the war, but local people formed preservation societies, revived them and still pass them on.
A summer event of Tokadai New Town, held every year in Tokadai Central Park, with bon-odori dancing, a flea market and food stalls. The 40th was held on 25–26 July 2026.

At the Ikenouchi festival a preservation society keeps up festival music, playing a piece called “Okagura” on flutes and drums, and there is also the “mikomai”, danced to it with bells and fans. At Fukugonji Temple in Okusa, a fire-walking ritual is held in midwinter: people follow the head priest across burning fire to purify body and mind. At the Sue district summer festival, Sue Elementary School’s wadaiko drum club performed.

The “Shinooka Ondo”, also called the “Shin-Shinooka Ondo”, is a local song bearing the Shinooka name, loved as a bon-odori staple. A recording posted on a video-sharing site shows that it was released as a record.

The citizens’ group Tokadai wo Kangaeru Kai has kept up the “Tokadai Music Festival” as a joint proposal project with the city’s Eastern District Development Office; November 2026 brings the 11th. The 7th, in November 2024 in the auditorium of the East Community Center, drew 240 people. At the 8th, in March 2025, a women’s choir and a residents’ band performed, and at the end the audience sang along. Tokadai Central Park also has an open-air stage, built in 2002.

The peach orchards on the eastern hills gave “Tokadai” (“peach-blossom heights”) its name, and the landscape (Kamisue) is one of Aichi Prefecture’s “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resources”. “Shinooka peaches” are known nationwide for their large, very sweet fruit. They have been grown in Kamisue, Takane, Okusa and nearby for about 80 years, and at Toryo Junior High School students cook with eastern peaches grown by a parent.

Grapes are widely grown alongside peaches in Kamisue, Takane, Okusa and nearby. Fifth graders at Hikarigaoka Elementary School pick grapes with the help of local grape farmers. The local “Eastern District Specialty PR Team” and grape farmers have held a parent-and-child Christmas wreath workshop using Komaki grapes, and at a local-produce cooking session people made grape juice from grape skins.

The city presents Nagoya Cochin chicken as a specialty of the eastern district. According to the Shinooka Karuta, it was bred by a former Owari domain samurai who moved to Ikenouchi, started keeping chickens and crossed breeds again and again. In connection with “Nagoya Cochin Day” on 10 March, a local group holds sessions in Toryo Junior High School’s cooking room to make hikizuri-nabe, a local dish. At a market in the east, food-truck dishes using Nagoya Cochin quickly sold out.

A winery in Noguchi, opened in April 2015 by the social welfare corporation AJU Jiritsu no Ie. People with disabilities do the work, from growing the grapes to making and selling the wine. A “Spring Wine Festival” was held there in May 2024. A project that turned the grape pomace left over from winemaking into bread and recipes, together with a local bakery, a university and the city, was also carried out as an Eastern District trial activity.

The Oyama River crosses the east and is a large river where five streams, including the Ikeshita and Shinzo, meet. Upstream, the “Firefly Village” (Oyama-higashi) has been laid out as a rest area, and from early to mid-June Genji fireflies — now rarely seen — fly about. This scene too is one of the “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resources”. Shinooka Elementary School raises fireflies from larvae and releases them into the Oyama River.

The endangered Mamenashi grows wild in Okusa. It is one of the “Tokai hill-zone plants” found only in the hills of the Tokai region, and the “Tara Mamenashi Village” has a walking path and signboards. Local groups hold viewing sessions in spring when it flowers and in autumn when it fruits.

A city park of about 28.2 hectares in Okusa. Besides the “Sorisuberi Hill” for sledding, the Wanpaku Adventure Plaza, the “Chibikko Animal Village” where children can touch animals, and the Rainbow Falls, it has a disc golf course, a park golf course and a barbecue area, and a monthly flower map shows what is in bloom. The view of its observation tower has been chosen by the prefecture as a “Beautiful Aichi Landscape Resource”. In summer 2024 a local group held a nature school here where parents and children observed insects and plants.

The baseball ground of the city’s sports complex in Kamisue, also called the “Shimin Kyūjō” (citizens’ ballpark). It was completed in 1988. The foul lines are 92 meters and center field 120 meters, with long-pile artificial turf, floodlights and an indoor practice area. The multipurpose ground next to it is used for softball, football (soccer) and athletics.

Why is the reorganization happening in FY2027?

The city states: "Given the declining number of students, there is no time to delay school reorganization — it must be carried out as soon as possible." As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the Shinooka area has fallen to less than half compared to 20 years ago. If current trends continue, by 2033 all elementary schools and Shinooka JHS are projected to have only one class per grade, raising concerns about insufficient numbers for group activities, sports events, and club activities.

In Phase 1 (FY2027), schools will be reorganized as follows: [Elementary] · Tokadai Higashi Elementary ← Shinooka, Hikarigaoka, Oshiro (Okusa & Shiroyama 3-chome) · Tokadai Nishi Elementary ← Momogaoka, Sue, Oshiro (Shiroyama 2nd/4th/5th-chome) [Junior High] · Tokadai Higashi JHS ← Shinooka JHS, Hikarigaoka JHS (except Shiroyama 4-chome) · Tokadai Nishi JHS ← Toryo JHS, Hikarigaoka JHS (Shiroyama 4-chome) The Oshiro Elementary district is split depending on the specific neighborhood.
How were the school districts for Shiroyama 3-chome and 4-chome decided?

The Oshiro Elementary district is being split between east and west, and Shiroyama 3-chome and 4-chome sit right on the dividing line. Their districts were decided after a briefing at Shiroyama Community Hall on July 27, 2025, and a survey, from July 28 to September 1, 2025, of parents in households with children of junior high school age or younger. ・Shiroyama 3-chome: 49 of 80 households replied (61.3%). 33 households (67.3%) preferred Hikarigaoka Elementary / Hikarigaoka JHS, and 16 (32.7%) Momogaoka Elementary / Toryo JHS. ・Shiroyama 4-chome: 21 of 33 households replied (63.6%). 16 households (76.2%) preferred Momogaoka Elementary / Toryo JHS, and 5 (23.8%) Hikarigaoka Elementary / Hikarigaoka JHS. Under the plan, Shiroyama 3-chome belongs to Tokadai Higashi Elementary and Tokadai Higashi JHS, and Shiroyama 4-chome to Tokadai Nishi Elementary and Tokadai Nishi JHS. (Revised draft of the Shinooka District School Reorganization Plan; the city's school reorganization page)

After Phase 1 (FY2027), if student numbers continue to decline, the east and west schools may be further combined into 1 elementary and 1 junior high, introducing integrated elementary-junior high education. The decision on Phase 2 will be based on outcomes of Phase 1.

School bus service is planned for eligible elementary students in the service area (commuting distance of 2 km or more, etc.) — fully free. · Morning route: 1 trip · Afternoon routes: Up to 3 trips (lower grades / upper grades / club days) · Cost: Fully covered by the city (free for students) For service area details and stops, see the School Bus page. Note: For Shiroyama 3rd & 4th-chome, if a family opts to change its designated school and the commute then exceeds 2 km, the school bus is NOT available.
How will junior high students commute?
Bicycle commuting is planned for junior high students. Details on safe routes and rainy-day arrangements will be studied and announced in due course.
What will happen to extracurricular clubs?

With more students after consolidation, a wider variety of club activities is expected. Currently some clubs cannot run due to low numbers at small schools. After consolidation, students should have more options. Specific clubs will be decided during preparation based on teacher staffing and facilities.
Will classes get bigger? Will there be more teachers?

In some grades, classes will get bigger. The maximum class size is 35 for every elementary grade and the first year of junior high, and 40 for the second and third years; like Aichi Prefecture, the city plans to lower the second and third years to 35 in stages from FY2026. The national government also changed the law in 2026, setting the junior high standard at 35 (phased in until FY2027). The city says that optimal size means the number of classes, not the number of children per class, and told the city council that a class size of about 21–25 children, large enough to allow classes to be reshuffled, needs to be secured (Council Proceedings). As for teachers, the city says staff numbers will rise with pupil numbers, that it is working with the prefecture for FY2027, and that it will run its education so that guidance and care for each child are not neglected. (The city's responses to the public comments; the city's answers at the June 2026 parents' briefings)
What support is there for children who are not attending school?

In the city council, the city has answered as follows. In FY2025, 735 children in Komaki were not attending school: 319 in elementary school and 416 in junior high. Through “Metaverse komaki”, a virtual space children can join from home as an avatar, the city lets them study, meet others and get advice; at home they can use the tablet lent by their school. The city is also considering opening a comprehensive education support center for children not attending school; using a closed school building is one of the options, but nothing has been decided. (Answers to general questions at the June and September 2026 sessions; see Council Proceedings)
What is being done about safety on the route to school?

Each school inspects its routes every year and responds with signs, green edge lines and similar measures. For the routes after the merger, the city says it will carry out the necessary work once the routes are formally designated, and that the budget for this has been secured. Watching over children is done by route-patrol volunteers; the city notes this is goodwill work and daily cover cannot be promised, and that it will step up recruitment as volunteer numbers fall. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Is anything being done about walking to school in extreme heat?

The city says heat protection matters regardless of the reorganization, and that recent extreme summers have to be dealt with city-wide. As one measure, it is installing water-bottle refill stations at schools in FY2026. (City's reply in the public comment results)
Can I drive my child to school on rainy days? What about parking at the school?

The city says children normally walk to school with their walking group, because school parking is limited and many cars coming in and out could lead to accidents involving children. However, driving is already allowed in special cases, such as when a child is unwell, and the city says such cases will be discussed one by one, mainly with the school. At Hikarigaoka Elementary School (the building Tokadai Higashi Elementary School will use), a visitor car park and a vehicle entrance are to be added on the southeast side of the playground, separate from the current main gate. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Will the children meet each other before the merger?

Yes. After the public comments, the plan was amended to schedule exchanges and joint activities between the schools beforehand, so children get used to the new setting. On 14 July 2026, 4th and 5th graders of the five elementary schools met for a joint exchange event at the East Community Center, and a joint event for every grade of the five schools is planned for October. The city also says it plans, for the elementary schools, hands-on arts and culture lessons with the Komaki Citizens Cultural Foundation and an exchange event in Tokadai Central Park, and for the junior high schools, joint satoyama (woodland) conservation work and an arts appreciation event for Shinooka and Hikarigaoka Junior High Schools. A "practice commute" is planned for February 2027, in which pupils then in years 1–5 will walk the new route or ride the bus from their designated stop. An exchange of “self-introduction cards” had first been considered for the first term, but it was dropped because of problems with it. Exchanges between particular schools or grades will also be held through field trips and integrated study time. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings; “Shinooka School Reorganization News” vol.6)
We worry about the effect on third-year students' grades and applications.

Teacher numbers follow a prefectural standard based on the number of classes, so the city says it cannot staff above that standard. Within that limit, it says it will keep working to place teachers from the former schools as evenly as possible. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Who decides the new schools' lessons and educational goals, and when?

A preparatory research committee for the school reorganization was set up in July 2025 and is discussing and deciding what the new schools need — curriculum, educational goals, school song, emblem, club activities and more. At the June 2026 parents' briefings, the new schools' educational goals and school life were explained. A joint school management council of the eight schools is planned for December 2026. The types and number of clubs will be decided during preparations, depending on teacher staffing and facilities after the reorganization. (Revised plan; “Shinooka School Reorganization News” Nos. 4 and 5)
Can uniforms and school supplies still be used?

The junior high uniform is not changing, so it can be handed down between siblings. The older uniforms (the stand-collar and sailor styles) are also allowed under the rules. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Which school cap should we buy? Can we keep using our current one?

There is no designated school cap at the new schools. Caps designated by the current schools can still be worn from April 2027. If you buy a new one, choose something easy to wear every day on the way to and from school. The city suggests three things to look for: ① a brim that blocks direct sunlight, ② easy to put on and take off, ③ a material that does not trap heat. Children starting school from April 2027 will hear more from their school at the new-pupil briefing. All current school supplies can still be used. Items printed with an old school name (such as tracksuits) will come in a new design when you buy or replace them. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
What happens to the special-needs classes and the Japanese-language room?

A special-needs class is capped at eight children; above that it becomes two or more classes. As for "Animo", the Japanese-language room at Oshiro Elementary, the city plans to move it elsewhere from FY2027 and will announce the location once decided. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Is there emotional support for children as their school changes?

The city recognizes that a big change of environment can weigh on children's minds and bodies. It says it will especially publicize and strengthen counseling by each school's counselors and school counselors before and after the reorganization, and pass on information and support methods for children who need support to the new schools. Exchanges so that children can meet before the reorganization are also under way (Q&A on exchanges). The city also told the city council that it is considering opening a comprehensive education support center for children who are not attending school, with closed school buildings as one candidate site (not yet decided; Council Proceedings). (The city's responses to the public comments)
What happens to the after-school childcare club (gakudō)?

A club is to be set up inside each of the two new elementary schools, Tokadai Higashi and Tokadai Nishi, prepared on the expectation that more children will use it. How to apply, which rooms it will use and other details have not been announced yet. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Can a child who walks to school carry a smartphone?

Bringing smartphones and similar devices to school is not allowed unless there is a special reason, and the city says this rule will stay the same after the reorganization. For children who ride the school bus, an app is being introduced to check boarding and getting off (School bus Q&A). (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
Will the junior high school trip destination change with the reorganization?

The city says that for the FY2027 school trips of Tokadai Higashi JHS and Tokadai Nishi JHS, it is preparing on the assumption that the destination will again be the Kanto region (the Tokyo area), as before. (Questions and answers from the June 2026 briefing at Hikarigaoka JHS)
Where are the security cameras on school routes? Will more streetlights be added?

Security cameras: The city says it does not publish where the cameras are, for security reasons. Moving or adding cameras for the reorganization is being coordinated with the agencies concerned, and will be considered with cost-effectiveness in mind. Streetlights: School routes are checked for safety every year, and where a security light or similar is needed, the school sends a request. The city says it responds to those requests after talks with the road administrator and others. (City's replies at the briefing at Shinooka JHS on June 7, 2026)
What will happen to the buildings of closing schools?
The school buildings are generally planned to be demolished. However, gymnasiums and school grounds are generally planned to be kept for local sports and community activities.
When a school closes, will it still be an evacuation shelter?

The city intends to keep maintaining the gymnasiums and grounds of closing schools from April 2027, because schools are important bases for local sport and disaster preparedness. They are therefore expected to remain designated as evacuation shelters and evacuation sites. How the school buildings and sites will be used is being considered by the relevant city departments. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)
What will happen to sports days and community events?

School-run sports days will be held at the consolidated schools. However, community events organized by local neighborhood associations (sports days, summer festivals, etc.) can continue independently. Maintaining links with former school districts' community events after consolidation is a topic for the preparation process.
Which buildings will the new schools use?

The new schools will use the current buildings of Hikarigaoka Elementary, Momogaoka Elementary, Hikarigaoka JHS, and Toryo JHS respectively. Details on renovations will be studied and announced in due course.
Has the public comment period ended?

Yes. The public comment period ran from November 10 to December 9, 2025, receiving 142 submissions from 55 people (submitters: 39 by email, 13 by fax, 1 by post, 2 in person). The city has published its responses and a revised plan on the official city website.
Can I still share my opinion with the city?

While the public comment period has closed, you can still share views by phone or in person at the School Reorganization Promotion Section (TEL: 0568-39-5261). For more details, visit the official city website.
Is information available in other languages?

Yes. Issues 1–5 of the "Shinooka School Reorganization News" have been translated into Spanish, Filipino (Tagalog), Vietnamese, Portuguese, and Chinese. Download them from the official city website. Issue 6 is so far available in Japanese only.
I could not attend the briefing. Can I read what was said?

For the June 2026 parent briefings, the city has published a summary record of the questions and answers for each venue. The questions and answers submitted on comment sheets, and the opinions and proposals, are published too. All of them are on the city's official pages.
Is there any explanation for families who are not comfortable in Japanese?

The city acknowledges that although the reorganization newsletter has been translated, it has not reached all the families concerned. It says it will now hand out flyers in plain Japanese and other languages directly through each school, and respond to individual worries. (City's reply at the June 2026 briefings)

"Starting in FY2027 is too soon. Talking it through matters more than meeting a deadline." The city's response (summary) The number of children aged 0–5 is already known, so the next six years can be projected quite accurately. Given how fast that number falls, there is no time to spare, and FY2027 is the earliest the change can be made. "It is moving ahead without enough notice to residents or their agreement. Take it back to the drawing board." The city's response (summary) Work on the city-wide school plan began in FY2023 and was explained at town meetings in FY2024. In FY2025 the city set up the "Think About Schools" meetings and held parent discussion meetings and public briefings. "Do not merge schools mechanically to hit a 12-class figure. Smaller classes give children more attention." The city's response (summary) "Appropriate size" refers to the number of classes, not the number of children in one class. The city is not against small classes. But where most years have only one class, pupils cannot be reshuffled and relationships become fixed. "The school is the center of the neighborhood. Lose it and the events, the disaster response and the community itself weaken." The city's response (summary) A school has many roles, but first of all it is an educational facility. The gym and the grounds are to be kept in principle as community facilities; the classroom buildings will in principle be demolished. Ties with the community are to be deepened through how the new schools are run. "Walking children through this heat is dangerous, and we worry about safety checks on the bus." The city's response (summary) The plan was amended to add a boarding-check system that lets parents and the school confirm a child got on, and a system to prevent children being left on board. On heat, the city treats it as a city-wide issue and is installing water-bottle refill stations at schools in FY2026, among other measures. What is the Shinooka School Reorganization Plan?

In the Shinooka area of eastern Komaki City, rapid population decline and aging school facilities have become serious challenges. As of 2025, the population aged 19 and under in the area has fallen to less than half compared to 20 years ago, and if current trends continue, it is projected that by 2033 all elementary schools and Shinooka Junior High School will have only one class per grade. In response to this situation, Komaki City has formulated this reorganization plan, viewing the entire Shinooka area as a unified learning community to enrich nine years of continuous education. The four post-reorganization schools will be collectively called "Shinooka Gakuen." The plan aims to consolidate the current 5 elementary and 3 junior high schools into 2 elementary and 2 junior high schools in FY2027. From everything we have examined, we picked the 10 points that matter most for judging the plan. 【Fact】 marks what rests on published material; 🔎 marks this site’s view. The plan itself Quality of education The number of children

1 The assumptions behind “one class per grade by 2033” are not shown 【Fact】The city expects every elementary school in the district and Shinooka Junior High to have one class per grade by 2033, and says the reorganization cannot wait. 🔎 Our view: Only the result of the projection is published; how births, moves in and out, and new housing were assumed is not. With the assumptions, residents could separate what cannot be changed from what policy could still change. More →

2 No criteria are given for moving on to Phase 2 (one elementary and one junior high school) 【Fact】Phase 2 — merging into one elementary and one junior high school and introducing integrated elementary–junior high education — is to be considered if numbers fall further after Phase 1, judged by how Phase 1 goes. 🔎 Our view: What level “falling further” means is not stated. Unless it is said first how Phase 1 will be measured, Phase 2 looks like a foregone conclusion. More →

3 The reasons for where the school-route lines are drawn are hard to read 【Fact】The school bus covers trips of 2 km or more plus areas chosen for local conditions, but Shiroyama 3 and 4-chome are not covered even where the district change makes the trip longer than 2 km. The usage guidelines were to be handed out at briefings, and applications ran from 30 August to 30 September 2026. 🔎 Our view: The same 2 km can be covered in one case and not in another, and the published materials do not make the reason clear. The application deadline also came before the guidelines were settled. More →

4 What happens to the closed school buildings is not set out together with the closure dates 【Fact】The use of the buildings that will close is left for future consideration in the published materials. Nationally, 74.4% of former school buildings still standing are being used for something else (MEXT survey, FY2024). 🔎 Our view: Schools are evacuation shelters and venues for local events. If closures go ahead before uses are decided, the area will be without that hub for a while. More →

5 Consensus-building is judged by how the process was designed, not by the number of comments 【Fact】The public comment period drew 142 comments from 55 people. The national guide revised in August 2026 asks both for careful, two-way discussion and for a timeline that does not keep putting off a decision. 🔎 Our view: Counting comments does not measure support or opposition. What matters is how people were reached, and at which stage what could still be changed. More →

6 There is no yardstick for checking whether learning and growth improve after the reorganization 【Fact】The city says lessons where children learn from each other need a group of a certain size, and lists the problems of small schools (no class reshuffles, few chances to take on roles, and so on). The city’s appropriate size is 12–24 classes per school. 🔎 Our view: What is shown is “the problems of today’s small schools”. We find no yardstick in the published materials for checking how attainment and personal growth change after the reorganization. More →

7 Class size after the merger depends heavily on how many pupils are in each year group 【Fact】The class-size cap is 35 (in the second and third years of junior high it has been 40 and is being lowered to 35 step by step until FY2027). When a year group exceeds the cap it is split into more classes, and teacher numbers are calculated from the number of classes (Act on Standards for Class Formation and Staff Numbers). The city says “optimal size” means the number of classes, not the number of pupils per class, and told the council it needs “class sizes of about 21–25 that allow classes to be reshuffled.” 🔎 Our view: The cap of 35 is “the line above which a year group is split”; it does not push classes towards that size. At today’s schools with one class per year group, a year group is under 35, so the cap has no effect on class size. Once merging enlarges a year group, 36 pupils become two classes of 18, but 70 pupils become two classes of 35. The same merger can leave one year group in classes of just over 20 and put another in classes at the cap. How “about 21–25” will be kept, and whether extra teachers will be added for the transition years, has not been said. More →

8 Support for children’s wellbeing in the transition, and for health and safety, is not yet visible 【Fact】The city sets out exchanges between schools before the merger, stronger counseling and handing on information about children who need support. School nurses are allotted basically one per school of three or more classes, and the gyms and grounds of closing schools are to stay as evacuation sites. 🔎 Our view: Going from eight schools to four also means going from eight nurse’s offices to four. How the exchanges will be judged sufficient, bus travel and admission for children needing medical care, and preparing for the school and the home evacuation site being different are not in the published materials. More →

9 Jobs increased, but children did not 【Fact】Establishments in the eastern district rose from 917 in 2009 to 1,095 in 2014, and employees from 12,388 to 20,671 (Eastern District Development Strategy). Meanwhile the district’s under-20 population is less than half of what it was 20 years ago. Most of Tokadai is zoned for detached houses only, and the Tokadai Line closed in 2006. 🔎 Our view: Child-rearing support that is the same anywhere in the city does little to decide which district people live in. We think the bigger factors were the lack of housing young households can move into and of ways to commute. More →

10 No department has “the number of children in the east” as its goal, and the tools the city can decide on itself go unused 【Fact】Responsibility is split: school reorganization lies with the Board of Education, eastern development and land use with the Urban Policy Department, child-rearing with the Children’s Future Department, and business location with the Regional Revitalization Department. The Tokadai district plan and the location optimization plan are plans the city decides itself. The revised national guide asks for planning together with town development, including the mayor’s departments. 🔎 Our view: The school reorganization section deals with the result of decline; it is not there to increase numbers. In our view, the urban-planning tools that would help the east most are the ones least used. More →

These are this site’s proposals, not something the city is considering. The evidence for each can be read via “More” on the In-depth page. Protect and raise the quality of education Increase the number of children in the east Carrying on our schools’ legacy

① Publish the yardsticks for learning first, and report every year 💡 Proposal: Before the reorganization, publish measures of attainment (such as the share of children who say they understand lessons, in a form that identifies no person or school), personal growth (such as the share who took on a role) and conditions (number of classes, grades where classes can be reshuffled, subjects with specialist teachers), and report on them every year. These can also serve as the criteria for Phase 2. More (evidence) →

② Add teachers for the transition years 💡 Proposal: Use the national and prefectural extra-teacher allocations heavily in the first years after the merger, combining small-group and ability-based teaching with passing on records of where children struggle. This answers concretely the worries of year groups whose classes get bigger. More (evidence) →

③ Link nine years of inquiry learning with the district’s real issues and data 💡 Proposal: Take the district’s own issues — the use of closed buildings, the bus service, the population outlook — and combine lessons that graph the city’s statistics and make forecasts, projects where every child takes a role, and chances to try things with local adults. This builds math, information skills and the ability to run a community together. More (evidence) →

④ Turn bus travel and disaster preparedness into lessons in independence and resilience 💡 Proposal: Hand children tasks suited to their grade, such as moving to the timetable and reporting days they will not ride. In the former school buildings kept as shelters, children, parents, the bus operator and the community draw up the disaster rules together. More (evidence) →

⑤ Plan health support by the number of children, not the number of schools 💡 Proposal: Before the new schools open, publish the number of school nurses at each, the school-doctor arrangements, and how children needing medical care will be admitted and travel by bus. Link fitness to make up for less walking, and heat measures, with health lessons. More (evidence) →

⑥ Publish the assumptions and targets, and make the number of children in the east a department’s goal 💡 Proposal: With the assumptions public, residents, businesses and the city can argue from the same figures. Put the eastern development council and the school reorganization discussions in the same forum, adopt the east’s child population as a shared indicator, and decide which department is responsible for it. More (evidence) →

⑦ Mix housing types as the new town changes generations 💡 Proposal: Review the district plan of detached houses only on plots of 150 m² or more, and turn the 166 vacant homes — the most in the city — into homes that families with children can move into, through renovation support and leasing. The prefecture and city should discuss regenerating the housing area the prefecture built within one framework. More (evidence) →

⑧ Treat commuting and school travel as a condition for settling 💡 Proposal: Children’s school buses and adults’ commutes are two sides of the same problem. In the city’s own survey, transport was among the top reasons young households gave for choosing where they moved. Consider roads and bus routes toward Kasugai and elsewhere together with housing policy. More (evidence) →

⑨ Make closing school sites hubs for families, and keep a high school as an option 💡 Proposal: Use the buildings nearest the district’s center for child-rearing support, after-school places and meeting space, making up for schools being further away. Before deciding on demolition, estimate once the conditions and costs of a high school as an option. More (evidence) →

⑩ Open doors for work other than factories and logistics, turning a “place to work” into a “place to live” 💡 Proposal: The city’s business-location subsidy requires at least 1,000 m² of floor space and 500 million yen of investment (100 million for SMEs), which IT, design and cultural work cannot reach. Create a small scheme measured by jobs, and workspaces in vacant homes and shops in the east, as a landing place for the settlement grant for people working in the city. More (evidence) →

⑪ Record the school songs and cheer songs, and keep them through streaming 💡 Proposal: Before the schools close, record each school’s song, anthems and cheer songs sung by today’s children, graduates and local people. After confirming permission from the lyricists and composers (or their rights holders) and the consent of those singing, make them available to anyone on music streaming services. More (evidence) →

⑫ Make time at the new schools to share the former schools’ songs 💡 Proposal: At Shinooka Gakuen events and exchange gatherings, set aside time to introduce the former schools’ songs. Apart from learning the new school song, telling children that “it is fine to treasure your old school’s song too” can support them emotionally. More (evidence) →

⑬ Archive school flags, records and the local karuta 💡 Proposal: Organize school flags, school histories, commemorative books, works and photos of events, display them in the remaining gyms or community facilities and publish them digitally too. Things a school has made out of local history and life, such as Shinooka Elementary’s “Shinooka Karuta”, can be handed on as material for play and learning at the new schools too. More (evidence) →

⑭ Carry on performing arts grown at school through “preservation societies,” as with bo-no-te 💡 Proposal: Like the bo-no-te preservation societies, have groups of graduates, parents and local people carry on Sue Elementary’s wadaiko, Hikarigaoka Elementary’s “Hikarikko Soran” happi coats and each school’s events. Decide who will carry them and how before the schools close, and link them to the new schools’ clubs, community clubs and local festivals. More (evidence) →

⑮ Link local festivals, specialties and history to learning at the new schools 💡 Proposal: Create chances for children at the new schools to join, across school district lines, the Tokadai Festival, the Ikenouchi festival, the bo-no-te shrine festivals and dances handed down locally such as the Shinooka Ondo. Learn about specialties such as peaches, grapes and Nagoya Cochin chicken from the producers in the Period for Integrated Studies and in cooking classes. Also let children learn the history of the Oyama Temple Ruins, a national historic site, and of the Shinooka kilns, a major pottery-producing area over a thousand years ago, through visits, hands-on experience and exhibits. You can put this site on the Home Screen of your phone or computer and use it like an app. Press the 📲 button (next to the language switcher in the header, and in the share box at the bottom of the page). It opens full-screen from the icon, without the address bar. It loads the latest content from the internet each time. With no connection, it shows only pages you have opened before, and says so. It sends no notifications. Visits are counted without cookies and without identifying anyone (see “About Visit Counts” on this page). To stop using it, delete it like any other app.

This site publishes new developments as a feed. Add it to a feed reader and new items reach you without opening the site. What you get: the city’s school reorganization notices, events of the Shinooka-area community councils, eastern district development news, and this site’s updates. How to subscribe: add the address below to a feed reader. Readers widely used in Japan include Feedly, Inoreader (with a Japanese interface), and NetNewsWire (free) or Reeder for iPhone, iPad and Mac. The format is Atom, which almost any RSS reader can read. Each item links to the matching corner of this site, not directly to the city’s individual pages. The feed is in Japanese, whatever display language you choose. https://komaki-east-school-reorg.github.io/feed.xml 📡 Follow updates by feed (RSS)

To see how this site is read and to make it easier to use, we count visits in a way that uses no cookies. What is counted: the page opened and the display language, which site you came from (the domain only), the screen size, which feature buttons are pressed (share, listen, etc.), and whether you came from a QR code. When you follow a link to another site, only the kind of destination (the city, a school, etc.) is counted; the page address is not sent. What is not counted: your name or email address, anything you type, the grade you choose, or whom you share with. No cookies and no number that identifies you are created. Counting uses GoatCounter, an open-source analytics service. No outside script is loaded. As with any connection, your IP address reaches the counting service. Nothing is counted when your browser is set to “do not track” (Do Not Track or Global Privacy Control). You can also turn counting off for this device with the button below.
